blocks.p: Satan, having circled the earth, returns by night as a mist into Paradise with his deceit already planned, and enters the serpent as it sleeps. In the morning Adam and Eve go out to their work, which Eve proposes to divide between them in different places, each working apart. Adam does not agree, pointing to the danger that the Enemy they were warned about might tempt her if he found her alone. Eve, unwilling to be thought not careful or firm enough, presses to go apart, all the more eager to put her strength to the test. Adam at last gives way. The serpent finds her alone. His subtle approach: first gazing, then speaking, with much flattery praising Eve above all other creatures. Eve, wondering to hear the serpent speak, asks how he came by human speech and an understanding he did not have before. The serpent answers that by tasting a certain tree in the garden he gained both speech and reason, which he had lacked until then. Eve asks him to bring her to that tree, and finds that it is the Tree of Knowledge, which is forbidden. The serpent, now grown bolder, with many wiles and arguments persuades her at length to eat. Pleased with the taste, she considers for a while whether to share it with Adam or not; at last she brings him some of the fruit and tells him what persuaded her to eat it. Adam is at first appalled, but seeing that she is lost, resolves through the strength of his love to perish with her, and, making light of the offense, eats the fruit too. Its effects on them both. They try to cover their nakedness; then they fall into quarreling and accuse each other.

v: No more of talk where God or angel guest
With man, as with his friend, familiar, used
To sit indulgent, and with him partake
Rural repast, permitting him meanwhile
Venial discourse unblamed: I now must change
Those notes to tragic; foul distrust, and breach
Disloyal on the part of man, revolt
And disobedience; on the part of Heaven,
Now alienated, distance and distaste,
Anger and just rebuke, and judgment passed,
That brought into this world a world of woe,
Sin and her shadow Death, and Misery,
Death’s harbinger. Sad task! yet argument
Not less but more heroic than the wrath
Of stern Achilles on his foe pursued
Three times in flight around Troy’s wall; or rage
Of Turnus for Lavinia, his betrothed;
Or Neptune’s ire, or Juno’s, that so long
Perplexed the Greek and Cytherea’s son;
If I can win a style to match the theme
From my celestial patroness, who deigns
Her nightly visitation unimplored,
And dictates to me slumbering, or inspires
My easy, unpremeditated verse:
Since first this subject for heroic song
Pleased me, long choosing, and beginning late;
Not eager by my nature to compose
Wars, until now the only argument
Deemed fit for epic, chief skill to dissect
With long and tedious havoc fabled knights
In battles feigned (the better fortitude
Of patience and heroic martyrdom
Unsung), or to describe races and games,
Or tilting gear, and shields with coats of arms,
Devices quaint, caparisons, and steeds,
Bases and tinsel trappings, gorgeous knights
At joust and tournament; then marshaled feast
Served in the hall by stewards, seneschals:
The skill of craft, or of a humble post,
Not that which justly gives heroic name
To person or to poem. I, in these
Not skilled nor studious, have a higher theme
Still left, sufficient of itself to raise
That name, unless an age too late, or cold
Climate, or years, should damp my rising wing,
Weighed down, as well they may, if all be mine,
Not hers who brings it nightly to my ear.
The sun had set, and after him the star
Of Hesperus, whose office is to bring
Twilight upon the earth, short arbiter
Of day and night; and now from end to end
Night’s hemisphere had veiled the horizon round,
When Satan, who had lately fled the threats
Of Gabriel out of Eden, now grown keen
In meditated fraud and malice, bent
On man’s destruction, heedless what might fall
Of worse upon himself, came fearless back.
By night he fled, and at midnight returned
From compassing the earth, wary of day,
Since Uriel, regent of the sun, had spied
His entrance, and forewarned the cherubim
That kept their watch; then, full of anguish, driven,
The space of seven continuous nights he rode
With darkness; thrice the equinoctial line
He circled; four times crossed the car of Night
From pole to pole, traversing each colure;
On the eighth came back, and on the coast that faced
Away from gate and cherub watch, by stealth
Found unsuspected way. There was a place,
Not now, though sin, not time, first wrought the change,
Where Tigris, at the foot of Paradise,
Into a gulf shot underground, till part
Rose up a fountain by the Tree of Life.
In with the river sank, and with it rose
Satan, wrapped in the rising mist; then sought
Where to lie hid. Sea he had searched, and land,
From Eden over Pontus, and the pool
Maeotis, up beyond the river Ob;
As far down as Antarctic; and in length
West from Orontes to the ocean barred
At Darien, then to the land where flow
Ganges and Indus: thus the orb he roamed
With searching care, and with inspection deep
Considered every creature, which of all
Most opportune might serve his wiles, and found
The serpent subtlest beast of all the field.
Him, after long debate, irresolute
In turning thoughts, his final judgment chose,
Fit vessel, fittest child of fraud, in whom
To enter, and his dark suggestions hide
From sharpest sight: for in the wily snake
Whatever tricks he played, none would suspect,
As from his wit and native subtlety
Proceeding, which, in other beasts observed,
Might breed a doubt of diabolic power
Active within, beyond the sense of brute.
Thus he resolved, but first, from inward grief,
His bursting passion poured out these laments:
“O Earth, how like to Heaven, if not preferred
More justly, seat more fit for gods, as built
With second thoughts, reforming what was old!
For what God, after better, would build worse?
Terrestrial heaven, danced round by other heavens
That shine, yet bear their bright attendant lamps,
Light above light, it seems, for you alone,
In you converging all their precious beams
Of sacred influence! As God in Heaven
Is center, yet extends to all, so you,
Centered, receive from all those orbs; in you,
Not in themselves, their virtue all appears,
Productive in herb, plant, and nobler birth
Of creatures animate with graded life
Of growth, sense, reason, all summed up in man.
With what delight could I have walked you round,
If I could find joy here: sweet interchange
Of hill and valley, rivers, woods, and plains,
Now land, now sea, and shores with forest crowned,
Rocks, dens, and caves! But I in none of these
Find place or refuge; and the more I see
Pleasures about me, so much more I feel
Torment within, as from the hateful siege
Of contraries; all good to me becomes
Bane, and in Heaven much worse would be my state.
But neither here I seek, no, nor in Heaven,
To dwell, unless by mastering Heaven’s Supreme;
Nor do I hope to be less miserable
By what I seek, but others to make such
As I, though it rebound the worse on me:
For only in destroying I find ease
To my relentless thoughts; and, he destroyed,
Or won to what may work his utter loss,
For whom all this was made, all this will soon
Follow, as linked to him in weal or woe:
In woe, then, that destruction wide may range!
To me shall be the glory, sole among
The infernal Powers, in one day to have marred
What he, Almighty called, six nights and days
Continued making, and who knows how long
Before had been contriving; though perhaps
Not longer than since I in one night freed
From shameful servitude almost one half
The angelic name, and thinner left the throng
Of his adorers. He, to be avenged,
And to repair his numbers thus impaired,
Whether such virtue, spent of old, now failed
More angels to create (if they at least
Are his created), or to spite us more,
Determined to advance into our room
A creature formed of earth, and him endow,
Exalted from so base an origin,
With heavenly spoils, our spoils. What he decreed
He carried out: made man, and for him built
This world magnificent, and earth his seat,
Pronounced him lord, and—O indignity!—
Subjected to his service angel wings,
And flaming ministers, to watch and tend
Their earthly charge. Of these the vigilance
I dread, and to elude it, wrapped in mist
Of midnight vapor, glide obscure, and pry
In every bush and brake, where chance may find
The serpent sleeping, in whose mazy folds
To hide me, and the dark intent I bring.
“O foul descent! that I, who once contended
With gods to sit the highest, now am forced
Into a beast, and, mixed with bestial slime,
This essence to incarnate and imbrute,
That to the height of deity aspired!
But what will not ambition and revenge
Descend to? Who aspires must sink as low
As high he soared, exposed, at first or last,
To basest things. Revenge, though sweet at first,
Soon bitter, back upon itself recoils;
Let it; I care not, so it lights well aimed,
Since higher I fall short, on him who next
Provokes my envy, this new favorite
Of Heaven, this man of clay, son of despite,
Whom, to spite us the more, his Maker raised
From dust: spite then with spite is best repaid.”
So saying, through each thicket, dank or dry,
Like a black mist low creeping, he held on
His midnight search, where soonest he might find
The serpent. Him, fast sleeping, soon he found,
In labyrinth of many a round self-rolled,
His head the midst, well stored with subtle wiles:
Not yet in horrid shade or dismal den,
Nor harmful yet, but on the grassy herb,
Fearless, unfeared, he slept. In at his mouth
The Devil entered, and the brute’s own sense,
In heart or head, possessing, soon inspired
With act of intellect; but still his sleep
Disturbed not, waiting close the approach of morn.
Now when the sacred light began to dawn
In Eden on the humid flowers, that breathed
Their morning incense, when all things that breathe
From earth’s great altar send up silent praise
To the Creator, and his nostrils fill
With grateful smell, out came the human pair
And joined their vocal worship to the choir
Of creatures wanting voice; that done, enjoy
The season, prime for sweetest scents and airs;
Then talk of how that day they best may ply
Their growing work; for much their work outgrew
The hands’ dispatch of two gardening so wide.
And Eve first to her husband thus began:
“Adam, well may we labor still to dress
This garden, still to tend plant, herb, and flower,
Our pleasant task enjoined; but till more hands
Aid us, the work under our labor grows,
Luxuriant by restraint: what we by day
Lop overgrown, or prune, or prop, or bind,
One night or two with wanton growth derides,
Tending to wild. Now, therefore, you advise,
Or hear the first thoughts that my mind presents:
Let us divide our labors; you where choice
Leads you, or need is most, whether to wind
The woodbine round this arbor, or direct
The clasping ivy where to climb, while I,
In that young growth of roses intermixed
With myrtle, find what to put right till noon.
For while so near each other thus all day
Our task we choose, what wonder if so near
Looks intervene, and smiles, or something new
Draws on casual talk, which interrupts
Our day’s work, brought to little, though begun
Early, and the hour of supper comes unearned?”
To whom thus Adam gave his mild reply:
“Sole Eve, sole partner, to me far beyond
Compare above all living creatures dear,
Well have you put it, well your thoughts employed
How we might best fulfill the work which here
God has assigned us; nor shall you lack praise
From me; for nothing lovelier is found
In woman than to study household good,
And good works in her husband to promote.
Yet not so strictly has our Lord imposed
Labor, as to debar us when we need
Refreshment, whether food, or talk between,
Food of the mind, or this sweet interchange
Of looks and smiles; for smiles from reason flow,
To brutes denied, and are of love the food,
Love not the lowest end of human life.
For not to irksome toil, but to delight
He made us, and delight to reason joined.
These paths and arbors, doubt not, our joint hands
Will keep from wilderness with ease, as wide
As we need walk, till younger hands in time
Assist us. But if too much talk perhaps
Should tire you, to short absence I could yield;
For solitude is sometimes best society,
And short retirement urges sweet return.
But other doubt possesses me, lest harm
Befall you severed from me; for you know
What we were warned of: how a spiteful power,
Envying our happiness, and of his own
Despairing, seeks to work us woe and shame
By sly assault; and somewhere close at hand
Watches, no doubt, with greedy hope to find
His wish and best advantage, us apart,
Hopeless to circumvent us joined, where each
To other speedy aid might lend at need;
Whether his first design be to withdraw
Our loyalty from God, or to disturb
Conjugal love, than which perhaps no bliss
Enjoyed by us excites his envy more;
Or this, or worse, leave not the faithful side
That gave you being, still shades you and protects.
The wife, where danger or dishonor lurks,
Safest and seemliest by her husband stays,
Who guards her, or with her the worst endures.”
To whom the virgin majesty of Eve,
As one who loves, and meets some unkindness,
With sweet, austere composure thus replied:
“Offspring of Heaven and Earth, and all earth’s lord,
That such an enemy we have, who seeks
Our ruin, I have learned, both told by you
And from the parting angel overheard,
As in a shady nook I stood behind,
Returned just as the evening flowers closed.
But that you should my firmness therefore doubt
To God or you, because we have a foe
May tempt it, I expected not to hear.
You fear not violence from him, since we,
Not capable of death or pain, are such
As cannot take it in, or can repel.
His fraud, then, is your fear, which plainly shows
Your equal fear that my firm faith and love
Can by his fraud be shaken or seduced:
Thoughts—how did they find harbor in your breast,
Adam—misjudging her to you so dear?”
To whom with healing words Adam replied:
“Daughter of God and man, immortal Eve,
For such you are, from sin and blame entire:
Not out of doubt of you do I dissuade
Your absence from my sight, but to avoid
The attempt itself, intended by our foe.
For he who tempts, though vainly, yet will stain
The tempted with a foul dishonor, thought
Not incorruptible in faith, not proof
Against temptation. You yourself with scorn
And anger would resent the offered wrong,
Though found in vain: do not misjudge me, then,
If such affront I labor to avert
From you alone, which on us both at once
The enemy, though bold, will hardly dare,
Or daring, first on me the assault shall light.
Nor should you scorn his malice and false guile:
Subtle he needs must be, who could seduce
Angels; nor think superfluous others’ aid.
I from the influence of your looks receive
Increase in every virtue; in your sight
More wise, more watchful, stronger, if need were
Of outward strength; while shame, you looking on,
Shame to be overcome or overreached,
Would rouse my utmost vigor, roused, unite.
Why should you not feel the same sense within
When I am present, and your trial choose
With me, best witness of your virtue tried?”
So spoke domestic Adam in his care
And matrimonial love; but Eve, who thought
Less credit given to her faith sincere,
Thus with sweet accent her reply renewed:
“If this is our condition, thus to dwell
In narrow circuit, hemmed in by a foe,
Subtle or violent, we not endowed
Singly with like defense, wherever met,
How are we happy, still in fear of harm?
But harm precedes not sin: only our foe,
Tempting, affronts us with his foul esteem
Of our integrity: his foul esteem
Sticks no dishonor on our brow, but turns
Foul on himself; then why be shunned or feared
By us, who rather double honor gain
From his surmise proved false, find peace within,
Favor from Heaven, our witness from the event?
And what is faith, love, virtue, if untried,
Alone, without exterior help sustained?
Let us not then suspect our happy state
Left so imperfect by the Maker wise
As not secure to single or combined.
Frail is our happiness, if this be so,
And Eden were no Eden, thus exposed.”
To whom thus Adam fervently replied:
“O woman, best are all things as the will
Of God ordained them; his creating hand
Nothing imperfect or deficient left
Of all that he created, much less man,
Or what might make his happy state secure,
Secure from outward force; within himself
The danger lies, yet lies within his power:
Against his will he can receive no harm.
But God left free the will; for what obeys
Reason is free; and reason he made right,
But bid her well beware, and stand erect,
Lest, by some fair-appearing good surprised,
She dictate false, and misinform the will
To do what God expressly has forbidden.
Not then mistrust, but tender love enjoins
That I should mind you often, and you me.
Firm we subsist, yet possible to swerve,
Since reason not impossibly may meet
Some specious object by the foe suborned,
And fall into deception unaware,
Not keeping strictest watch, as warned to do.
Seek not temptation, then, which to avoid
Were better, and most likely if from me
You sever not: trial will come unsought.
If you would prove your constancy, then prove
Obedience first; the other who can know,
Not seeing you attempted, who attest?
But if you think trial unsought may find
Us both less guarded than, thus warned, you seem,
Go; for your stay, not free, absents you more;
Go in your native innocence; rely
On what you have of virtue; summon all;
For God toward you has done his part: do yours.”
So spoke the patriarch of mankind; but Eve
Persisted; yet, submissive, though last, replied:
“With your permission, then, and thus forewarned
Chiefly by what your own last reasoning words
Touched only, that our trial, when least sought,
May find us both perhaps far less prepared,
More willingly I go, nor much expect
A foe so proud will first the weaker seek;
If so, his rout will shame him all the more.”
Thus saying, from her husband’s hand her hand
Softly she drew, and like a wood nymph light,
Oread or dryad, or of Delia’s train,
Went to the groves; but Delia herself
Surpassed in gait and goddesslike demeanor,
Though not, as she, with bow and quiver armed,
But with such gardening tools as art yet rude,
Guiltless of fire, had formed, or angels brought.
To Pales or Pomona, thus adorned,
Likest she seemed, Pomona when she fled
Vertumnus, or to Ceres in her prime,
Yet virgin of Proserpina by Jove.
Her long with ardent look his eye pursued,
Delighted, but desiring more her stay.
Often to her his charge of quick return
He gave again; she just as often pledged
To be returned by noon amid the bower,
And all things in best order to invite
Noontide repast, or afternoon’s repose.
O much deceived, much failing, hapless Eve,
In your presumed return! perverse event!
You never from that hour in Paradise
Found either sweet repast or sound repose;
Such ambush, hid among sweet flowers and shades,
Waited with hellish rancor, imminent,
To intercept your way, or send you back
Despoiled of innocence, of faith, of bliss.
For now, and since first break of dawn, the Fiend,
Mere serpent in appearance, had come out,
And on his quest, where likeliest he might find
The only two of mankind, but in them
The whole included race, his purposed prey.
In bower and field he sought, where any tuft
Of grove or garden plot lay pleasantest,
Their tending, or their planting for delight;
By fountain or by shady rivulet
He sought them both, but wished his luck might find
Eve separate; he wished, but not with hope
Of what so seldom chanced; when, to his wish,
Beyond his hope, Eve separate he spies,
Veiled in a cloud of fragrance, where she stood,
Half seen, so thick the roses, bushing round
About her, glowed; stooping again to prop
Each flower of slender stalk, whose head, though gay,
Crimson, purple, azure, or flecked with gold,
Hung drooping, unsupported; these she stays
Gently with myrtle bands, heedless meanwhile
Herself, though fairest unsupported flower,
From her best prop so far, and storm so near.
Nearer he drew, and many a walk traversed
Of stateliest covert, cedar, pine, or palm;
Then gliding, bold, now hidden and now seen
Among thick-woven shrubberies and flowers
Embroidered on each bank, the hand of Eve:
Spot more delicious than those gardens feigned
Of the revived Adonis, or renowned
Alcinous, host of old Laertes’ son,
Or that, not mythic, where the sapient king
Held dalliance with his fair Egyptian spouse.
Much he the place admired, the person more.
As one who long in populous city pent,
Where houses thick and sewers foul the air,
Walks out upon a summer’s morn to breathe
Among the pleasant villages and farms
Nearby, from each thing met conceives delight,
The smell of grain, or tedded grass, or cows,
Or dairy, each rural sight, each rural sound;
If, nymphlike, some fair maiden chance to pass,
What pleasing seemed, for her now pleases more,
She most, and in her look sums all delight:
Such pleasure took the serpent to behold
This flowery plot, the sweet retreat of Eve,
Thus early, thus alone. Her heavenly form,
Angelic, but more soft and feminine,
Her graceful innocence, her every air
Of gesture or least action, overawed
His malice, and with sweet violence robbed
His fierceness of the fierce intent it brought:
That while the Evil One stood drawn away
From his own evil, and for the time remained
Stupidly good, of enmity disarmed,
Of guile, of hate, of envy, of revenge.
But the hot Hell that always in him burns,
Though in mid-Heaven, soon ended his delight,
And tortures him now more, the more he sees
Of pleasure not for him ordained: then soon
Fierce hate he recollects, and all his thoughts
Of mischief, welcoming them, thus excites:
“Thoughts, where have you now led me, with what sweet
Compulsion thus transported, to forget
What brought us here—hate, not love, nor the hope
Of Paradise for Hell, hope here to taste
Of pleasure, but all pleasure to destroy,
Save what is in destroying; joy besides
To me is lost. Then let me not let pass
Occasion which now smiles: behold, alone
The woman, opportune for all attempts;
Her husband (for I view far round) not near,
Whose higher intellect I shun the more,
And strength, of courage haughty, and of limb
Heroic built, though of terrestrial mold,
A foe not to be scorned, exempt from wound,
I not; so much has Hell debased, and pain
Enfeebled me, to what I was in Heaven.
She fair, divinely fair, fit love for gods,
Not terrible, though terror be in love
And beauty, not approached by stronger hate,
Hate stronger, under show of love well feigned:
The way which to her ruin now I tend.”
So spoke the Foe of all mankind, enclosed
In serpent, evil inmate, and toward Eve
Addressed his way, not with a zigzag wave,
Prone on the ground, as since, but on his rear,
Circular base of rising folds, that towered
Fold above fold, a surging maze; his head
Crested aloft, and carbuncle his eyes;
With burnished neck of verdant gold, erect
Amid his circling spires, that on the grass
Floated in waves: and pleasing was his shape,
And lovely; never since of serpent kind
Lovelier: not those that in Illyria changed
Hermione and Cadmus, or the god
In Epidaurus; nor to which transformed
Ammonian Jove, or Capitoline, was seen,
He with Olympias, this with her who bore
Scipio, the height of Rome. With track oblique
At first, as one who sought access, but feared
To interrupt, sidelong he works his way.
As when a ship, by skillful steersman worked
Near river’s mouth or foreland, where the wind
Veers often, often tacks and shifts her sail,
So varied he, and of his twisting train
Curled many a wanton wreath in sight of Eve,
To lure her eye. She, busy, heard the sound
Of rustling leaves, but did not mind, as used
To such light sport before her through the field
From every beast, more ready at her call
Than at Circean call the herd disguised.
He, bolder now, uncalled before her stood,
But gazing, as admiring; often bowed
His turret crest and sleek enameled neck,
Fawning, and licked the ground on which she trod.
His gentle, dumb expression turned at length
The eye of Eve to mark his play; he, glad
Of her attention gained, with serpent tongue
Organic, or by impulse of the air,
His fraudulent temptation thus began:
“Wonder not, sovereign mistress, if perhaps
You can, who are sole wonder; much less arm
Your looks, the heaven of mildness, with disdain,
Displeased that I approach you thus, and gaze
Insatiate, I alone; nor have I feared
Your solemn brow, more solemn thus withdrawn.
Fairest resemblance of your Maker fair,
You all things living gaze on, all things yours
By gift, adore your heavenly beauty, viewed
With ravishment, and best would be beheld
Where universally admired. But here,
In this wild enclosure, among these beasts,
Beholders crude, too shallow to discern
Half what in you is fair, one man except,
Who sees you—and what is one?—who should be seen
A goddess among gods, adored and served
By angels numberless, your daily train.”
So fawned the Tempter, and his prelude tuned;
Into the heart of Eve his words made way,
Though at the voice much marveling; at length,
Not unamazed, she thus in answer spoke:
“What may this mean? Language of man pronounced
By tongue of brute, and human sense expressed?
The first, at least, of these I thought denied
To beasts, whom God on their creation day
Created mute to all articulate sound;
The second I hold doubtful; in their looks
Much reason, and in their acts, often shows.
You, serpent, subtlest beast of all the field
I knew, but not with human voice endowed;
Redouble, then, this miracle, and say
How you have gained your speech, once mute, and how
To me so friendly grown above the rest
Of brutish kind that daily are in sight?
Say, for such wonder claims attention due.”
To whom the guileful Tempter thus replied:
“Empress of this fair world, resplendent Eve,
Easy for me it is to tell you all
That you command, and right you should be obeyed.
I was at first as other beasts that graze
The trodden herb, of abject thoughts and low,
As was my food, and knew no more than food
Or sex, and apprehended nothing high;
Till on a day, roaming the field, I chanced
A goodly tree far distant to behold,
Laden with fruit of fairest colors mixed,
Ruddy and gold. I nearer drew to gaze;
When from the boughs a savory odor, blown,
Grateful to appetite, more pleased my sense
Than smell of sweetest fennel, or the teats
Of ewe or goat dropping with milk at eve,
Unsucked by lamb or kid, intent on play.
To satisfy the sharp desire I had
Of tasting those fair apples, I resolved
Not to defer; hunger and thirst at once,
Powerful persuaders, quickened at the scent
Of that alluring fruit, urged me so keen.
Around the mossy trunk I soon was wound,
For high from ground the branches would demand
Your utmost reach, or Adam’s. Round the tree
All other beasts that saw, with like desire
Longing and envying stood, but could not reach.
Up in the tree at last, where plenty hung
Tempting so near, to pluck and eat my fill
I spared not; for such pleasure till that hour
At pasture or at spring I never found.
Sated at length, before long I perceived
Strange alteration in me, to degree
Of reason in my inward powers; and speech
Was not long wanting, though this shape remained.
From then to speculations high or deep
I turned my thoughts, and with capacious mind
Considered all things visible in heaven,
Or earth, or air between, all fair and good;
But all that fair and good in your divine
Semblance, and in your beauty’s heavenly ray,
United I beheld; and none to yours
Equivalent or second; which compelled
Me thus, though troublesome perhaps, to come
And gaze, and worship you, by right declared
Sovereign of creatures, mistress of the world.”
So talked the spirited sly snake; and Eve,
Yet more amazed, unwary, thus replied:
“Serpent, your overpraising leaves in doubt
The virtue of that fruit, in you first proved.
But say, where grows the tree? from here how far?
For many are the trees of God that grow
In Paradise, and various, yet unknown
To us; in such abundance lies our choice
As leaves a greater store of fruit untouched,
Still hanging incorruptible, till men
Grow up to their provision, and more hands
Help to unburden Nature of her yield.”
To whom the wily adder, blithe and glad:
“Empress, the way is ready, and not long:
Beyond a row of myrtles, on a flat,
Close by a fountain, one small thicket past
Of flowering myrrh and balm; if you accept
My guidance, I can quickly bring you there.”
“Lead, then,” said Eve. He, leading, swiftly rolled
In tangles, and made intricate seem straight,
To mischief swift. Hope elevates, and joy
Brightens his crest; as when a wandering fire,
Compact of oily vapor, which the night
Condenses, and the cold environs round,
Kindled through agitation to a flame
(Which, it is said, some evil spirit attends),
Hovering and blazing with delusive light,
Misleads the amazed night-wanderer from his way
To bogs and mires, and many a pond or pool,
There swallowed up and lost, far from all aid:
So glittered the dire snake, and into fraud
Led Eve, our credulous mother, to the tree
Of prohibition, root of all our woe;
Which when she saw, thus to her guide she spoke:
“Serpent, we might have spared our coming here,
Fruitless to me, though fruit be here to excess,
The credit of whose virtue rest with you,
Wondrous indeed, if cause of such effects.
But of this tree we may not taste nor touch;
God so commanded, and left that command
Sole daughter of his voice; the rest, we live
Law to ourselves; our reason is our law.”
To whom the Tempter guilefully replied:
“Indeed? Has God then said that of the fruit
Of all these garden trees you shall not eat,
Yet lords declared of all in earth or air?”
To whom thus Eve, yet sinless: “Of the fruit
Of each tree in the garden we may eat;
But of the fruit of this fair tree amid
The garden, God has said, ‘You shall not eat
Of it, nor shall you touch it, lest you die.’”
She scarce had said, though brief, when, now more bold,
The Tempter, but with show of zeal and love
To man, and indignation at his wrong,
New part puts on, and, as to passion moved,
Sways, as disturbed, yet comely, and in act
Raised, as of some great matter to begin.
As when of old some orator renowned
In Athens or free Rome, where eloquence
Flourished, since mute, to some great cause addressed,
Stood in himself collected, while each part,
Motion, each act won hearing before words,
At times began at full height, as no delay
Of preface brooking, through his zeal of right:
So standing, moving, or to full height grown,
The Tempter, all impassioned, thus began:
“O sacred, wise, and wisdom-giving plant,
Mother of science! Now I feel your power
Within me clear, not only to discern
Things in their causes, but to trace the ways
Of highest agents, deemed however wise.
Queen of this universe, do not believe
Those rigid threats of death; you shall not die.
How should you? By the fruit? It gives you life
To knowledge. By the Threatener? Look on me,
Me, who have touched and tasted, yet both live,
And life more perfect have attained than fate
Meant me, by venturing higher than my lot.
Shall that be shut to man which to the beast
Is open? Or will God incense his ire
For such a petty trespass, and not praise
Rather your dauntless virtue, whom the pain
Of death pronounced, whatever death may be,
Deterred not from achieving what might lead
To happier life, knowledge of good and evil?
Of good, how just? Of evil—if what is evil
Be real, why not known, since easier shunned?
God therefore cannot hurt you, and be just;
Not just, not God; not feared then, nor obeyed:
Your fear itself of death removes the fear.
Why then was this forbidden? Why, but to awe,
Why but to keep you low and ignorant,
His worshipers? He knows that on the day
You eat of it, your eyes that seem so clear,
Yet are but dim, shall perfectly be then
Opened and cleared, and you shall be as gods,
Knowing both good and evil, as they know.
That you should be as gods, since I as man,
Internal man, is but proportion due:
I, of brute, human; you, of human, gods.
So you shall die perhaps, by putting off
Human, to put on gods—death to be wished,
Though threatened, which no worse than this can bring.
And what are gods, that man may not become
As they, by sharing in a godlike food?
The gods are first, and that advantage use
On our belief, that all from them proceeds;
I question it; for this fair earth I see,
Warmed by the sun, producing every kind;
Them, nothing. If they made all, who enclosed
Knowledge of good and evil in this tree,
So that whoever eats at once attains
Wisdom without their leave? And in what lies
The offense, that man should thus attain to know?
What can your knowledge hurt him, or this tree
Impart against his will, if all is his?
Or is it envy? And can envy dwell
In heavenly breasts? These, these, and many more
Causes declare your need of this fair fruit.
Human goddess, reach out, then, and freely taste.”
He ended, and his words, replete with guile,
Into her heart too easy entrance won.
Fixed on the fruit she gazed, which to behold
Might tempt alone; and in her ears the sound
Still rang of his persuasive words, infused
With reason, to her seeming, and with truth.
Meanwhile the hour of noon drew on, and waked
An eager appetite, raised by the smell
So savory of that fruit, which, with desire,
Inclined by now to touch it or to taste,
Solicited her longing eye; yet first,
Pausing a while, thus to herself she mused:
“Great are your virtues, doubtless, best of fruits,
Though kept from man, and worthy to be admired,
Whose taste, too long forborne, at first attempt
Gave elocution to the mute, and taught
The tongue not made for speech to speak your praise.
Your praise he also who forbids your use
Conceals not from us, naming you the Tree
Of Knowledge, knowledge both of good and evil;
Forbids us then to taste; but his forbidding
Commends you more, while it implies the good
By you communicated, and our want:
For good unknown, sure, is not had; or, had
And yet unknown, is as not had at all.
Put plainly, what does he forbid but knowing,
Forbid us good, forbid us to be wise?
Such prohibitions bind not. But if death
Binds us with after-bands, what profits then
Our inward freedom? On the day we eat
Of this fair fruit, our doom is, we shall die.
How dies the serpent? He has eaten, and lives,
And knows, and speaks, and reasons, and discerns,
Irrational till then. For us alone
Was death invented? Or to us denied
This intellectual food, for beasts reserved?
For beasts it seems: yet that one beast which first
Has tasted envies not, but brings with joy
The good befallen him, no suspect source,
Friendly to man, far from deceit or guile.
Then what am I to fear—or know to fear,
Under this ignorance of good and evil,
Of God or death, of law or penalty?
Here grows the cure of all, this fruit divine,
Fair to the eye, inviting to the taste,
Of virtue to make wise: what hinders, then,
To reach, and feed at once both body and mind?”
So saying, her rash hand in evil hour
Forth reaching to the fruit, she plucked, she ate.
Earth felt the wound, and Nature from her seat,
Sighing through all her works, gave signs of woe
That all was lost. Back to the thicket slunk
The guilty serpent, and well might; for Eve,
Intent now wholly on her taste, naught else
Regarded; such delight till then, it seemed,
In fruit she never tasted, whether true
Or fancied so, through expectation high
Of knowledge; nor was godhead from her thought.
Greedily she engorged without restraint,
And knew not she ate death. Sated at length,
And heightened as with wine, in jocund mood,
Thus to herself she happily began:
“O sovereign, virtuous, precious of all trees
In Paradise, of blessed power to give
Wisdom, till now obscured, and in ill fame,
And your fair fruit let hang, as to no end
Created; but henceforth my early care,
Not without song, each morning, and due praise,
Shall tend you, and the fertile burden ease
Of your full branches, offered free to all;
Till, dieted by you, I grow mature
In knowledge, as the gods who all things know;
Though others envy what they cannot give;
For had the gift been theirs, it would not here
Have grown. Experience, next to you I owe,
Best guide: not following you, I had remained
In ignorance; you open wisdom’s way,
And give access, though secret she retire.
And I perhaps am secret; Heaven is high,
High and remote, to see from there distinctly
Each thing on earth; and other cares perhaps
May have diverted from continual watch
Our great Forbidder, safe with all his spies
About him. But to Adam in what light
Shall I appear? Shall I to him make known
As yet my change, and give him leave to share
Full happiness with me, or rather not,
But keep the odds of knowledge in my power
Without a partner? so to add what lacks
In female sex, the more to draw his love,
And render me more equal, and perhaps,
A thing not undesirable, one day
Superior: for inferior, who is free?
This may be well; but what if God has seen,
And death ensue? Then I shall be no more,
And Adam, wedded to another Eve,
Shall live with her enjoying, I extinct:
A death to think! Confirmed, then, I resolve
Adam shall share with me in bliss or woe:
So dear I love him, that with him all deaths
I could endure, without him live no life.”
So saying, from the tree her step she turned,
But first low reverence done, as to the power
That dwelt within, whose presence had infused
Into the plant its knowing sap, derived
From nectar, drink of gods. Adam meanwhile,
Waiting, desirous of her coming, wove
Of choicest flowers a garland to adorn
Her tresses, and her rural labors crown,
As reapers often crown their harvest queen.
Great joy he promised to his thoughts, and new
Solace in her return, so long delayed;
But many times his heart, divining ill,
Misgave him; he the faltering rhythm felt;
And forth to meet her went, the way she took
That morn when first they parted. By the Tree
Of Knowledge he must pass; there he met her,
Scarce from the tree returning; in her hand
A bough of fairest fruit, that downy smiled,
New gathered, and ambrosial smell diffused.
To him she hastened; in her face excuse
Came prologue, and apology to prompt,
Which with bland words at will she thus addressed:
“Have you not wondered, Adam, at my stay?
You I have missed, and thought it long, deprived
Of your sight—agony of love till now
Not felt, nor shall be twice; for nevermore
Will I attempt what, rash, untried, I sought:
The pain of absence from your sight. But strange
Has been the cause, and wonderful to hear:
This tree is not, as we are told, a tree
Of danger tasted, nor to evil unknown
Opening the way, but of divine effect
To open eyes, and make them gods who taste;
And tasted, has proved such: the serpent, wise,
Or not restrained as we, or not obeying,
Has eaten of the fruit, and has become,
Not dead, as we are threatened, but from then
Endowed with human voice and human sense,
Reasoning to admiration; and with me
Persuasively has so prevailed, that I
Have also tasted, and have also found
The effects to correspond: opener my eyes,
Dim till now, dilated spirits, ampler heart,
And growing up to godhead; which for you
Chiefly I sought, without you can despise.
For bliss, as you have part, to me is bliss,
Tedious, unshared with you, and odious soon.
So you must also taste, that equal lot
May join us, equal joy, as equal love;
Lest, you not tasting, different degree
Disjoin us, and I then too late renounce
Deity for you, when fate will not permit.”
Thus Eve, with cheerful face, her story told;
But in her cheek a feverish flushing glowed.
Adam, for his part, soon as he had heard
The fatal trespass done by Eve, amazed,
Stood thunderstruck and blank, while horror chill
Ran through his veins, and all his joints relaxed;
From his slack hand the garland wreathed for Eve
Dropped down, and all the faded roses shed.
Speechless he stood and pale, till thus at length
First to himself he inward silence broke:
“O fairest of creation, last and best
Of all God’s works, creature in whom excelled
Whatever can to sight or thought be found,
Holy, divine, good, amiable, or sweet!
How are you lost! how on a sudden lost,
Defaced, deflowered, and now to death consigned!
Rather, how have you yielded to transgress
The strict forbiddance, how to violate
The sacred fruit forbidden! Some cursed fraud
Of our foe has beguiled you, still unknown,
And me with you has ruined; for with you
Certain my resolution is to die.
How can I live without you, how forgo
Your sweet converse, and love so dearly joined,
To live again in these wild woods forlorn?
Should God create another Eve, and I
Another rib supply, yet loss of you
Would never leave my heart. No, no! I feel
The link of nature draw me: flesh of flesh,
Bone of my bone you are, and from your state
Mine never shall be parted, bliss or woe.”
So having said, as one from sad dismay
Recomforted, and, after thoughts disturbed,
Submitting to what seemed past remedy,
Thus in calm mood his words to Eve he turned:
“Bold deed you have presumed, adventurous Eve,
And peril great provoked, who thus have dared,
Had it been only coveting to eye
That sacred fruit, sacred to abstinence,
Much more to taste it, under ban to touch.
But what is past, or done, who can undo?
Not God omnipotent, nor fate. Yet so
Perhaps you shall not die; perhaps the deed
Is not so heinous now: foretasted fruit,
Profaned first by the serpent, by him first
Made common, unhallowed, before we tasted,
Nor yet on him found deadly; he still lives,
Lives, as you said, and gains, to live as man,
Higher degree of life: inducement strong
To us, as likely, tasting, to attain
Proportional ascent, which cannot be
But to be gods, or angels, demigods.
Nor can I think that God, Creator wise,
Though threatening, will in earnest so destroy
Us, his prime creatures, dignified so high,
Set over all his works, which, in our fall,
For us created, must with us then fail,
Dependent made; so God shall uncreate,
Be thwarted, do, undo, and labor lose:
Not well conceived of God; who, though his power
Creation could repeat, yet would be loath
Us to abolish, lest the Adversary
Triumph and say, ‘Fickle their state whom God
Most favors; who can please him long? Me first
He ruined, now mankind; whom will he next?’
Matter of scorn, not to be given the Foe.
Whatever comes, with you I’ve fixed my lot,
Certain to undergo like doom; if death
Consort with you, death is to me as life;
So forcible within my heart I feel
The bond of nature draw me to my own,
My own in you; for what you are is mine;
Our state cannot be severed; we are one,
One flesh; to lose you were to lose myself.”
So Adam; and thus Eve to him replied:
“O glorious trial of exceeding love,
Illustrious evidence, example high!
Engaging me to emulate; but, short
Of your perfection, how shall I attain,
Adam, from whose dear side I boast I sprang,
And gladly of our union hear you speak,
One heart, one soul in both? Of which good proof
This day affords, declaring you resolved,
Sooner than death, or what than death is worse,
Shall separate us, linked in love so dear,
To undergo with me one guilt, one crime,
If such there be, in tasting this fair fruit;
Whose virtue (for of good still good proceeds,
Direct, or by occasion) has presented
This happy trial of your love, which else
So eminently never had been known.
Did I think death, as threatened, would ensue
This my attempt, I would alone sustain
The worst, and not persuade you; rather die
Deserted, than oblige you with a deed
Pernicious to your peace, chiefly assured
Remarkably so late of your so true,
So faithful love unequaled. But I feel
Far otherwise the outcome: not death, but life
Augmented, opened eyes, new hopes, new joys,
Taste so divine, that what of sweet before
Has touched my sense seems flat to this, and harsh.
On my experience, Adam, freely taste,
And fear of death deliver to the winds.”
So saying, she embraced him, and for joy
Tenderly wept, much won that he his love
Had so ennobled, as of choice to incur
Divine displeasure for her sake, or death.
In recompense (for such compliance bad
Such recompense best merits), from the bough
She gave him of that fair enticing fruit
With liberal hand. He scrupled not to eat,
Against his better knowledge, not deceived,
But fondly overcome with female charm.
Earth trembled from her entrails, as again
In pangs, and Nature gave a second groan;
Sky darkened, muttering thunder; some sad drops
Wept at completing of the mortal sin
Original; while Adam took no thought,
Eating his fill, nor Eve to iterate
Her former trespass feared, the more to soothe
Him with her loved society; that now,
As with new wine intoxicated, both
They swim in mirth, and fancy that they feel
Divinity within them breeding wings
With which to scorn the earth. But that false fruit
Far other operation first displayed,
Carnal desire inflaming; he on Eve
Began to cast lascivious eyes, she him
As wantonly repaid; in lust they burn,
Till Adam thus to dalliance urged Eve:
“Eve, now I see you are exact of taste,
And elegant, of wisdom no small part,
Since to each meaning savor we apply,
And palate call judicious. I the praise
Yield you, so well this day you have provided.
Much pleasure we have lost, while we abstained
From this delightful fruit, nor known till now
True relish, tasting; if such pleasure be
In things to us forbidden, it might be wished
For this one tree, ten trees had been forbidden.
But come, so well refreshed, now let us play,
As fits us, after such delicious fare;
For never did your beauty, from the time
I saw you first and wedded you, adorned
With all perfections, so inflame my sense
With ardor to enjoy you, fairer now
Than ever—bounty of this virtuous tree!”
So said he, and forbore no glance or touch
Of amorous intent, well understood
By Eve, whose eye darted contagious fire.
Her hand he seized, and to a shady bank,
Thick overhead with verdant roof embowered,
He led her, nothing loath; flowers were the couch,
Pansies, and violets, and asphodel,
And hyacinth, earth’s freshest, softest lap.
There they their fill of love and love’s delight
Took largely, of their mutual guilt the seal,
The solace of their sin, till dewy sleep
Oppressed them, wearied with their amorous play.
Soon as the force of that fallacious fruit,
That with exhilarating vapor bland
About their spirits had played, and inmost powers
Made err, was now exhaled, and grosser sleep,
Bred of unnatural fumes, with conscious dreams
Encumbered, now had left them, up they rose
As from unrest, and, each the other viewing,
Soon found their eyes how opened, and their minds
How darkened. Innocence, that as a veil
Had shadowed them from knowing ill, was gone;
Just confidence, and native righteousness,
And honor, from about them, naked left
To guilty Shame: he covered, but his robe
Uncovered more. So rose the Danite strong,
Herculean Samson, from the harlot lap
Of the Philistine Delilah, and woke
Shorn of his strength: they destitute and bare
Of all their virtue. Silent, and in face
Confounded, long they sat, as stricken mute,
Till Adam, though not less than Eve abashed,
At length gave utterance to these words constrained:
“O Eve, in evil hour you gave your ear
To that false worm, by whomsoever taught
To counterfeit man’s voice: true in our fall,
False in our promised rising; since our eyes
Opened we find indeed, and find we know
Both good and evil, good lost and evil got:
Bad fruit of knowledge, if this be to know,
Which leaves us naked thus, of honor void,
Of innocence, of faith, of purity,
Our wonted ornaments, now soiled and stained,
And in our faces evident the signs
Of foul concupiscence; hence, ills in store,
Even shame, the last of evils; of the first
Be sure, then. How shall I behold the face
Henceforth of God or angel, once with joy
And rapture often seen? Those heavenly shapes
Will dazzle now this earthly shape, their blaze
Insufferably bright. O might I here
In solitude live savage, in some glade
Obscured, where highest woods, impenetrable
To star or sunlight, spread their shadow broad,
And brown as evening! Cover me, you pines!
You cedars, with innumerable boughs
Hide me, where I may never see them more!
But let us now, as in bad plight, devise
What best may for the present serve to hide
The parts of each from other, that seem most
To shame exposed, and unseemliest seen:
Some tree, whose broad smooth leaves, sewn together
And girded on our loins, may cover round
Those middle parts, that this newcomer, Shame,
May not sit there, reproaching us unclean.”
So counseled he, and both together went
Into the thickest wood; there soon they chose
The fig tree, not that kind renowned for fruit,
But such as at this day, to Indians known,
In Malabar or Deccan spreads her arms,
Branching so broad and long, that in the ground
The bended twigs take root, and daughters grow
About the mother tree, a pillared shade
High overarched, and echoing walks between;
Where often Indian herdsmen, shunning heat,
Shelter in cool, and tend their pasturing herds
At loopholes cut through thickest shade. Those leaves
They gathered, broad as Amazonian shields,
And with what skill they had, together sewed,
To gird their waist; vain covering, if to hide
Their guilt and dreaded shame! O how unlike
To that first naked glory! Such of late
Columbus found the American, so girt
With feathered cincture, naked else and wild,
Among the trees on isles and wooded shores.
Thus fenced, and, as they thought, their shame in part
Covered, but not at rest or ease of mind,
They sat down there to weep; nor only tears
Rained at their eyes, but high winds worse within
Began to rise, high passions, anger, hate,
Mistrust, suspicion, discord, and shook sore
Their inward state of mind, calm region once
And full of peace, now tossed and turbulent:
For understanding ruled not, and the will
Heard not her voice, both in subjection now
To sensual appetite, who from beneath,
Usurping over sovereign reason, claimed
Superior sway. From thus distempered breast,
Adam, estranged in look and altered style,
His interrupted speech to Eve renewed:
“I wish that you had heeded me, and stayed
With me, as I implored you, when that strange
Desire of wandering, this unhappy morn,
From who knows where possessed you! We had then
Remained still happy, not as now, despoiled
Of all our good, shamed, naked, miserable.
Let none henceforth seek needless cause to prove
The faith they owe; when earnestly they seek
Such proof, conclude they then begin to fail.”
To whom, soon moved with touch of blame, thus Eve:
“What words have passed your lips, Adam severe!
Do you impute that to my fault, or will
Of wandering, as you call it, which who knows
But might as ill have happened with you by,
Or to yourself perhaps? Had you been there,
Or here the attempt, you could not have discerned
Fraud in the serpent, speaking as he spoke;
No ground of enmity between us known,
Why he should mean me ill, or seek to harm.
Was I then never to have left your side?
As well have grown there still a lifeless rib.
Being as I am, why did not you, the head,
Command me absolutely not to go,
Going into such danger as you claimed?
Too yielding then, you did not much object;
No, you permitted, sanctioned, kindly dismissed.
Had you been firm and fixed in your dissent,
Neither had I transgressed, nor you with me.”
To whom then, first incensed, Adam replied:
“Is this the love, is this the recompense
Of mine to you, ungrateful Eve, expressed
Immutable when you were lost, not I,
Who might have lived and known immortal bliss,
Yet willingly chose rather death with you?
And am I now upbraided as the cause
Of your transgressing? Not enough severe,
It seems, in your restraint! What more could I do?
I warned you, I admonished you, foretold
The danger, and the lurking enemy
That lay in wait; beyond this had been force,
And force upon free will has here no place.
But confidence then bore you on, secure
Either to meet no danger, or to find
Matter of glorious trial; and perhaps
I also erred in overmuch admiring
What seemed in you so perfect, that I thought
No evil dared attempt you; but I rue
That error now, which has become my crime,
And you the accuser. Thus it shall befall
Him who, to worth in women overtrusting,
Lets her will rule: restraint she will not brook,
And, left to herself, if evil then ensue,
She first his weak indulgence will accuse.”
Thus they in mutual accusation spent
The fruitless hours, but neither self-condemning,
And of their vain contest appeared no end.

blocks.p: Venial (5). Pardonable; the friendly talk with the angel guest Raphael in Books V–VIII.
Achilles … Troy’s wall (14–16). In Homer’s Iliad, Achilles in his wrath chased Hector three times around the walls of Troy.
Turnus … Lavinia (17). In Virgil’s Aeneid, Turnus raged when Lavinia, promised to him, was given to Aeneas.
Neptune’s ire … Juno’s … Cytherea’s son (18–19). Neptune harried the Greek Odysseus on his voyage home; Juno pursued Aeneas, son of Venus (Cytherea).
celestial patroness (21). Milton’s heavenly Muse, Urania of Book VII.
Devices … caparisons … Bases (35–36). Shield emblems with mottoes; ornamental cloths for horses; the embroidered skirts of mounted knights.
seneschals (38). Stewards of great medieval households, who ordered the feasts.
an age too late, or cold / Climate (44–45). Milton feared the world was in decline and that England’s cold climate dulled genius.
Hesperus (49). The evening star.
the threats / Of Gabriel (53–54). Gabriel drove Satan out of Eden at the end of Book IV.
equinoctial line … car of Night … colure (64–66). The equator; Night’s chariot; the colures are two great circles through the celestial poles. Satan kept to the earth’s shadow by circling the globe.
Pontus … Maeotis … Ob (77–78). The Black Sea, the Sea of Azov, and the great river of Siberia.
Orontes … Darien (80–81). A river of Syria; the Isthmus of Panama. The source text misprints “Orantes.”
subtlest beast of all the field (86). Genesis’s own description of the serpent [Gen. 3:1].
imbrute (166). Make bestial; lower to the level of a brute.
Oread or dryad … Delia (387). Mountain nymph or tree nymph; Delia is Diana, born on Delos, the huntress with bow and quiver.

Pales … Pomona … Vertumnus … Ceres … Proserpina (393–396). Roman goddesses of flocks and of fruit trees; the god of the seasons who wooed Pomona; the goddess of grain, before she bore Proserpina to Jove.
Adonis … Alcinous … Laertes’ son (440–441). The garden of Adonis, who revived each year; the orchard of Alcinous, king of the Phaeacians, who welcomed Ulysses, son of Laertes.
the sapient king … Egyptian spouse (442–443). Solomon and Pharaoh’s daughter, whose garden was real, not mythical [1 Kings 3:1; Song 6:2].
tedded grass (450). Mown grass spread out to dry.
carbuncle (500). A glowing red gem.
Hermione and Cadmus … Epidaurus (506–507). Cadmus and his wife Harmonia (Hermione) were changed to serpents in Illyria; Aesculapius, god of healing at Epidaurus, appeared as a serpent.
Ammonian Jove … Capitoline … Scipio (508–510). Jupiter Ammon in serpent form was said to have fathered Alexander the Great on Olympias, and Capitoline Jupiter to have fathered Scipio Africanus.
Circean (522). The enchantress Circe turned men into beasts that fawned on her.
Organic, or by impulse of the air (530). Either using the serpent’s tongue as an organ of speech, or moving the air directly.
spirited (613). Possessed by a spirit.
wandering fire (634). The will-o’-the-wisp, a marsh light said to lead night travelers astray.
Sole daughter of his voice (653). The one command God gave; the phrase echoes the Hebrew bath kol, “daughter of the voice,” a voice from heaven.
Has God then said (656–663). The exchange follows Genesis almost word for word [Gen. 3:1–3].
science (680). Knowledge.
you shall be as gods (708–709). The serpent’s promise in Genesis [Gen. 3:4–5].
Fair to the eye … she ate (777–781). Eve’s reasoning and act as Genesis gives them [Gen. 3:6].
flesh of flesh, / Bone of my bone (914–915). Adam’s first words over Eve, recalled now; compare “One flesh” (959) [Gen. 2:23–24].
not deceived … fondly (998–999). Adam sinned knowingly [1 Tim. 2:14]; “fondly” means foolishly, out of doting love.
savor … palate call judicious (1019–1020). A pun: Latin sapere means both “to taste” and “to be wise,” so sapience is both wisdom and taste.
the Danite … Samson … Delilah (1059–1062). Samson of the tribe of Dan woke shorn of his strength after Delilah betrayed him [Judg. 16:4–20].
The fig tree … Malabar or Deccan (1101–1103). The banyan of southern India, whose hanging branches root to form new trunks [Gen. 3:7].
Amazonian shields (1111). The shields of the Amazons, legendary women warriors.
Columbus … cincture (1116–1117). A belt or girdle of feathers, as worn by peoples Columbus met in the Caribbean.
